description:
We are a couple of individuals that finally realized our potential and capabilities to help space travellers who are concerned about their safety and well-being.
We're stubborn when it comes to obstacles, and hungry for finding the solution to break that obstacle. 
This is Helixion
summary:
Astronaut Self-Assessment Panel is a self-monitoring web app for crews on long space missions, built by team HELIXION. It runs in any browser, works offline, installs like an app, and is available in nine languages.

Astronauts answer one question per slide about vitals, symptoms, a quick reaction test and optional blood values. After every answer they see a green, yellow or red status and simple self-care steps. There are no medicines and no doses, and red always means contacting the flight surgeon. A readiness ring and body map show which body systems need attention first. The app also builds a personal baseline, so it flags changes from each person’s own normal.

The app uses NASA open data. A Live NASA catalog searches the Open Science Data Repository (OSDR). Real Inspiration4 crew data (OSD-575, OSD-569, OSD-635) is shown next to a person’s own values.

This addresses the challenge of health monitoring software for astronauts. When no doctor is nearby, crews need a clear way to notice problems early and act. It is a prototype, not a diagnosis, and its reference zones need review by a flight surgeon.
details:
What it does and how it works
The Astronaut Self-Assessment Panel is a web app that lets crew members check their own health on a long mission, when no doctor is nearby. The guided check-up asks one question per slide: vitals, symptoms, a reaction test and optional blood values. After each answer the app shows a green, yellow or red status and simple self-care steps. Red always says to contact the flight surgeon. There are no medicines and no doses. At the end a readiness ring and a body map show which body systems need attention first. The app also builds a personal baseline from each user’s own earlier values, so it can flag changes from their own normal.

NASA data

  • The Inspirations tab shows real Inspiration4 crew data from NASA OSDR studies OSD-575, OSD-569 and OSD-635. The check-up lab slides show crew ranges next to the user’s own value.
  • A Live NASA catalog searches OSDR directly and lists studies and their files.

Benefits and intended impact

  • A crew member gets a clear, quick view of their health and the next step, even offline.
  • Everything the user enters stays in their own browser.
  • The app is meant to help crews notice problems early and understand them. It can also help anyone far from a clinic on Earth. It is a prototype and not a diagnosis.

Tools and technology

  • Code: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step.
  • Offline and installable: a service worker makes it work offline and installable.
  • Cloudflare Workers: one relays NASA requests, and another sends daily reminders.
  • Hosting and source: GitHub and GitHub Pages.
  • Testing: 20 automated test files run with Node. Playwright and headless Chrome tested the app on desktop and phone sizes.
  • Hardware: no special hardware. It runs on any phone or computer with a browser.
  • AI assistance: we used Claude (Anthropic) to help write and review code, tests, translations, the print option and documentation. The team chose the idea, directed the work, checked the results and made the final decisions.

What is creative about it

  • A readiness ring and a body map replace long lists of numbers.
  • The check-up compares each person with their own baseline and with real crew data.
  • It has an animated space-themed design, a night mode, haptic and sound feedback, and nine languages.
  • The reaction test is a small game that gives a measurement.

Factors we considered

  • Safety: the app never diagnoses or suggests medicines. The reference zones are prototype values that a flight surgeon must review.
  • Honest data: missing answers show as “no data”, never green. The NASA crew data covers only four people, so we show it descriptively and draw no conclusions.
  • Privacy: health values stay in the browser. The reminder relay stores only the device’s push address, chosen time, time zone and language.
  • Accessibility: status uses symbols and patterns as well as colour. There are text size, contrast and night options, and touch-friendly buttons.
  • Reliability: it works offline, and the bundled NASA data is used when the live connection fails.
